meta.tagline: Azulejo blue, the Douro's wine and a city of bridges

pills: One of the world's most beautiful bookshops

overview.title: Welcome to Porto
overview.intro: Porto stopped standing in Lisbon's shadow long ago: this granite city built on the Douro tells its own story with blue-tiled churches, façades of rusty beauty and the wine lodges lined up across the river. Ribeira's coloured houses lean on the water, the iron bridge carries the signature of Eiffel's student, and the gulls bring the smell of the ocean into town. Porto is not polished — and that is exactly why it is warm. Accept the hills: every climb's reward is a view, and every descent ends in a glass of wine.

local_word.definition: The nickname of Porto's people: 'tripe eater'. Legend says the city gave all its meat to the explorers setting sail and kept only the tripe for itself. A Porto local carries the name with pride — a badge of sacrifice and stubbornness.

rules.title: Respect the hills, wear comfortable shoes
rules.description: Porto is a steep city: climbing from the river to the cathedral is a small ascent, and the cobbles slip in the rain. Wear trainers and treat the hills as excuses for breaks — every stop has either a café or a view.

rules.title: The port wine ritual is on the other bank
rules.description: The wine lodges are not in Porto but across the river in Vila Nova de Gaia. Walk over the bridge's upper deck, take a cellar tour and time the tasting for sunset — the river view comes with the glass.

rules.title: The francesinha is a full meal — don't underestimate it
rules.description: The city's legendary sandwich is a monument of meat, sausage, ham, cheese and beer sauce: chips beside it, an egg on top. Eat it at lunch and leave the evening empty — even the Tripeiros keep to one a day.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Metro line E to centre ~30 min

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: The Andante card works on the whole network

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: The lodges are on the Gaia bank

tip.label: The Porto philosophy
tip.text: In Porto you plan around the river: upper town in the morning, riverbank at noon, the far shore in the evening. Whichever way you walk you end up at the Douro — the city was designed that way.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The centre is walkable but hilly; the metro is modern, the historic tram is for pleasure, and the funiculars are friends of the knee.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: Metro line E (purple) reaches Trindade in half an hour: buy an Andante card at the machine, load it, use it across the network. Taxis run near a flat rate, but with the metro standing there, unnecessary.

items.title: The metro and the Andante card
items.description: A clean six-line network: Casa da Música, Trindade and São Bento are the knots. The same card works on trams and buses — mind the zone system; most sightseeing stays within Z2.

items.title: Historic tram line 1
items.description: The wooden tram runs along the river from Ribeira to Foz at the ocean's mouth: Porto's most beautiful half-hour ride. The nostalgia fare is higher than a normal ticket — the view pays it back.

items.title: Funiculars and the cable car
items.description: The Guindais funicular lifts you from Ribeira to the upper town in a minute; the Gaia cable car links the lodge district to the bridge top. Both short, both scenic — protect your knees.

items.title: On foot — bridge and banks
items.description: The upper deck of the Dom Luís I bridge belongs to pedestrians: the best walk between the two banks. Between the Ribeira quay, the Gaia bank and the miradouros, the city is solved on foot.

callout.label: Bridge tip
callout.text: Cross the Dom Luís I upper deck twice: towards Gaia by day (descending to the lodges), towards Porto in the evening (as the city lights come on). The same bridge, two entirely different photographs.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Porto, bank and altitude are everything: Ribeira at the river's edge, Baixa the city's heart, artistic Cedofeita, oceanside Foz.

local_word.definition: Portugal's blue-and-white tile art: in Porto, churches, stations and ordinary apartment blocks are clad in them. The hall of São Bento station is a museum of 20,000 tiles — even on your own street you're sure to find a few façades.

items.name: Ribeira
items.description: The UNESCO quarter of coloured houses leaning on the river: bridge views, quay cafés, street musicians. Tourist crowds and steep lanes are part of the bargain — the classic for a first visit.

items.name: Baixa (around Aliados)
items.description: The grand Aliados boulevard, São Bento station and the shopping streets: walk everywhere, hotels for every budget. The practical centre where the city's daily life crosses the tourist route.

items.name: Cedofeita and the arts district
items.description: Around the gallery street Miguel Bombarda: concept shops, brunch cafés, young Porto. Ten minutes from the centre, the soul of a neighbourhood — design guesthouse territory.

items.name: The Vila Nova de Gaia bank
items.description: The bank of the lodges and river terraces: your window faces the Porto skyline and the wine houses are next door. Calmer than Porto in the evenings — the view photographer's base.

items.name: Foz do Douro
items.description: The elegant seaside district where the river meets the ocean: a lighthouse, an esplanade walk, beach cafés. Half an hour to the centre by tram — for those after a city + ocean balance.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: In this Atlantic city the weather is moody and the light always beautiful: spring and September are gold, June is festival, winter green and calm.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Open-Air Opening
items.subtitle: Spring · Terraces, river breeze
items.description: The rains thin out, the quay cafés bring out their tables, and the Douro valley turns its brightest green. The crowds are not yet at summer levels — the ideal balance for walking and tasting.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: In May take the day train into the Douro valley: the Régua line hugs the riverbank, and with the vines fresh green the carriage window is a painting. Close with a tasting in Gaia on the way back.

items.label: Summer
items.name: São João Fever
items.subtitle: Summer · Festival, ocean cool, full quays
items.description: On the night of 23-24 June, São João turns the whole city into one street party: plastic hammers, grilled sardines, fireworks. July and August are hot, but the Atlantic breeze keeps Porto cooler than Lisbon.

callout.label: São João tip
callout.text: If you're there on São João night, don't resist the plan: take a plastic hammer, smile when you're bopped on the head, follow the sardine smoke. Ending at dawn on the Foz seafront with the sunrise is the tradition.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Harvest Light
items.subtitle: Autumn · Harvest season, a golden river
items.description: September is harvest month in the Douro: valley tours fill with vintage excitement and the city stays warm. In October and November the rain returns, but the misty river mornings are the city at its most photogenic.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: During the harvest some Douro quintas welcome guests to grape-treading: your feet turn purple and the story lasts a lifetime. Go up the valley by train and plan the return by boat.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Green and Quiet
items.subtitle: Winter · Rain, empty streets, cellar warmth
items.description: Atlantic rain washes the city, but prices fall, the streets return to the locals and the lodge tours know no season. When the sun breaks between showers, the granite streets shine — the photographer's winter.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: Turn a rainy day into an indoor chain: the Lello bookshop (first slot of the morning), the São Bento tiles, a cellar tour and a fado night. Porto's winter, done in the right order, is as full as its summer.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Porto's kitchen was built on working-class generosity: big portions, honest plates, wine always on the table.

local_word.definition: 'Little French girl': the Porto sandwich that buries layers of meat, sausage and ham under melted cheese and sits in a beer-and-tomato sauce. The name is dainty, the thing itself monumental — every Tripeiro has a 'best francesinha' address and an endless argument about it.

items.name: Francesinha — the city's monument
items.description: The layered meat sandwich under its melted-cheese blanket and famous sauce: every house guards its sauce recipe as a secret. Chips beside, an egg on top if you're brave — eat it at lunch and cancel dinner.
items.tag: A lunch mission · the sauce is a secret

items.name: Bacalhau and grilled sardines
items.description: Salted cod (bacalhau) is Portugal's national passion: on every menu à Brás or com natas. In summer the smell of grilled sardines holds the streets — on bread, eaten with your hands.

items.name: Tripas à moda do Porto
items.description: The dish that named the city: tripe slow-cooked with white beans and sausage. Not touristy — historic. For brave palates, the badge of a true Tripeiro.
items.tag: For the brave · the city's name comes from this pot

items.name: Pastel de nata + galão
items.description: A custard tart hot from the oven, cinnamon on top, milky coffee (galão) beside it: the opening ceremony of a Porto morning. Judge not by the yellow in the window but by the hour it left the oven.

items.name: Port tasting — the Gaia lodges
items.description: Tawny, Ruby, Vintage: tastings among century-old casks in the lodges across the river. The small family lodges are calmer and more generous than the big brands — choose by asking.
items.tag: On the Gaia bank · time it for sunset

items.name: Bolhão market and petiscos
items.description: In the restored historic market: cheese, olives and smoked-meat stalls with standing tastings — the heart of petiscos, Portugal's answer to tapas. Go before noon and never skip the stallholder chat.
items.tag: In the historic market · chat included

callout.label: Wine tip
callout.text: Don't assume port is only a sweet liqueur: dry white port + tonic is the city's summer aperitif and a local classic most visitors never hear of. Ask for the 'dry white' at your tasting — that's where the prejudice breaks.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone knows Lello; these six are Porto's backstage.

items.name: Miradouro da Vitória
items.description: From the terrace at the end of the old Jewish quarter's narrow lanes, the cathedral, the river and the Gaia lodges sit in one frame: at sunset the local youth gathers with beers in hand. Free, uncrowded, unforgettable.

items.rarity: A tiled cathedral of a hall
items.name: São Bento station
items.description: The station hall tells Portugal's history in 20,000 azulejos: wars, weddings, harvests. No train ticket needed — go early in the morning and see the hall empty. The city's most beautiful 'waiting room'.

items.rarity: A blue waterfall on a church wall
items.name: Capela das Almas
items.description: A chapel clad head to toe in tiles in the middle of the Santa Catarina shopping street: its blue-and-white façade is azulejo art's street-level peak. Small inside, iconic outside — shoot it in morning light.

items.name: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal
items.description: Gardens descending to the river terrace by terrace: peacocks, magnolias and a different Douro view at every corner. The city's most generous green space for picnics and sunsets.

items.name: Casa da Música
items.description: Koolhaas's concrete diamond is the city's contemporary icon: the guided tour takes you backstage and into the tiled VIP room. Evening concert tickets are often surprisingly cheap — check the programme.

items.name: The Foz lighthouse and esplanade
items.description: Tram 1 to the river's mouth: at the Felgueiras lighthouse the waves pound the stones, and the esplanade cafés face the ocean. A wave show on stormy days, a sunset classic on calm ones.

callout.label: Lello tip
callout.text: If you're going into Lello, buy the ticket online and stand at the door at opening: the first half hour is the only slot where photos are possible. The ticket price is deducted from any book — pick your souvenir there.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Porto is hospitable; its traps are small, but knowing them saves both budget and time.

items.name: Losing a midday to the Lello queue
items.description: At midday the bookshop queue reaches an hour and the inside turns to rush-hour metro: the famous staircase disappears behind the crowd.
items.instead: Go at opening or near closing, ticket bought in advance. If you hit peak hours, let it go — the São Bento tiles and the Vitória view give the same joy without the queue.

items.name: Dinner on the Ribeira quay
items.description: The riverside tables tax the view: lukewarm bacalhau at tourist prices.
items.instead: Have only a glass of wine on the quay; eat two streets uphill or in Baixa's tascas. The same river view is often cheaper on the Gaia side.

items.name: Walking into the first lodge
items.description: The biggest brands at the bridge exit run on large tour groups: the tasting is rushed and the price pays for the logo.
items.instead: Walk five minutes uphill: in the small family lodges the guide has time for you and the tasting pour is more generous. Book in the morning, taste at sunset.

items.name: A tuk-tuk for a short hop
items.description: The tuk-tuks waiting on the squares sell a 15-minute walking route at tour prices.
items.instead: The centre is walked anyway; for the steep hills there are the funicular and the cable car. If you do want a tuk-tuk, choose a genuinely long route like a Foz sunset run and fix the price first.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Porto every river-facing table charges a view tax, yet the best views are free — the bridge deck, the miradouros, the Gaia quay. Watch the view for nothing; spend the money on wine and the bakery.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From tiles to wine, a two-bank day

steps.title: São Bento + pastel de nata
steps.description: See the station's tiled hall while it's empty; start the day at the corner bakery with a hot nata + galão.

steps.title: The cathedral and the upper town
steps.description: A first river view from the Sé's terrace; descend the narrow lanes to the Vitória miradouro and meet the city from above.

steps.title: The francesinha mission
steps.description: Face the city's monument sandwich at lunch: dunking bread in the sauce is allowed. A walk afterwards is mandatory — the plan is built that way.

steps.title: Ribeira and the bridge crossing
steps.description: Coffee on the coloured quay, then walk the Dom Luís I upper deck to Gaia: the river beneath your feet, the skyline before you.

steps.title: A lodge tasting
steps.description: Tour + tasting at a small family lodge: start with a Tawny, be surprised by the dry white. On the way out, claim your sunset spot on the Gaia quay.

steps.title: Evening in Baixa
steps.description: Bacalhau or a petiscos crawl at a tasca; afterwards the bars of the Galerias de Paris street — a Porto night starts modestly and ends late.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: City, ocean and valley — three Portos

steps.title: Classic Porto
steps.description: The one-day flow above: São Bento, cathedral, francesinha, bridge, lodge.

steps.title: Art and ocean
steps.description: Lello at opening and the Carmo tiles in the morning; the Cedofeita galleries + Bolhão market at noon; tram 1 to Foz in the afternoon — lighthouse, esplanade and an ocean sunset.

steps.title: The Douro valley
steps.description: Morning train to Pinhão or Régua: vine terraces, a quinta tasting, a river boat ride; back to Porto in the evening and a farewell view from Vitória.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Porto's Portuguese accent is throaty and warm; these five open doors and bakery counters.

items.meaning: Hello / good morning — the mandatory opener of every exchange
Thank you — ends in -o if you're male, -a if you're female
Please — 'se faz favor' sounds even more local in Porto
Cheers! — as the glasses rise with port
'Cool, great' — the approval word the young fit into every sentence
